task: Write one sentence of your own using the word avarice. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know avarice should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: What began as careful saving hardened into avarice: he charged his own sister interest on lunch money and logged every gift he gave as a debt owed back.
Greed stops short of avarice — greed can be a moment's overreach at the buffet, while avarice is a settled, lifelong hunger for wealth.
Rapacity goes further than avarice — the avaricious hoard what comes to them, but rapacity reaches out and takes, plundering like a bird of prey.

Covetousness is desire aimed at one particular thing that belongs to someone else — a colleague's corner office, a rival's title. Avarice is broader and colder: a general, consuming hunger for money and possessions themselves, whoever holds them. Covetousness has a target; avarice has an appetite.

Miserliness is the refusal to spend or share what you already have — the hoarder clutching a full purse. Avarice is the hungering side of the same vice: an endless drive to gain more wealth, whether or not any of it is ever enjoyed. The miser guards; the avaricious grasp.

Avarice means excessive greed.

The heiress owned four empty mansions yet sued a neighbor over a strip of lawn no wider than a doormat; her lawyers called it principle, but the town called it avarice — wealth chasing more wealth long after need had ended.
Avarice is stronger than ordinary greed for a reason: greed can be a passing appetite, while avarice names greed grown into a ruling passion, a fixed hunger for money that crowds out everything else.
Avarice is the moralist's word — at home in sermons, fables, and closing arguments.
In casual speech say greed; choose avarice when you want greed to sound like a permanent vice that has taken charge of a life rather than a bad afternoon at the buffet.

When the freight magnate Odile Renn died, the appraisers expected a mansion of treasures.
They found warehouses instead: silver services still in factory crates, four hundred clocks nobody had wound, deeds to buildings she had never once visited.
Her ledgers told the same story of avarice — every page a purchase, hardly a page of use.
She had not loved any of it, her secretary admitted; she had loved the acquiring, and each acquisition only sharpened the appetite for the next.
The estate sale lasted eleven days, and the crates went to buyers who at least intended to open them.
